issues.text: The Windows example named here is the one case where the rule stated right after it is false. A path beginning with a single separator is completed with the DRIVE of the working directory, not with the working directory: on SDK 10.0.300 with the working directory F:\SourceCode\lo-trinh-architect, Path.GetFullPath(@"\demo\app.conf") returns F:\demo\app.conf, not F:\SourceCode\lo-trinh-architect\demo\app.conf. The docs say such a path is "relative from the root of the current drive". The clause is also past depth_notes for an L1 lesson (see scope.beyond_scope).
issues.quote: Any other path is relative, including one that starts with a bare separator on Windows, and the operating system measures it from the working directory before it looks.
issues.fix: Delete the Windows sub-case so the sentence reads: "Any other path is relative, and the operating system measures it from the working directory before it looks." If the case must stay, split it: "On Windows a path that begins with a bare separator is still relative, but it is completed with only the drive of the working directory."

issues.text: The two failures are presented as strictly ordered (existence first, permission second), which does not hold when the folder itself is closed to the process. In the stage-0 lab box, user `dev` reading /tmp/probe/closed/absent.txt, where `closed` exists at mode 700 owned by root, gets "Permission denied" for a file that does not exist. The lesson's own hedge "two common ways" is in the following sentence, but the mechanism sentence states the order without a condition.
issues.quote: If nothing is at the resulting path, the answer is `not found` … If something is there, one more check happens
issues.fix: Condition the order: "If the folder can be searched and nothing is at the resulting path, the answer is `not found`, and that message names the path actually tried. If something is there — or if the folder itself is closed to this process — one more check happens: …"

issues.text: "at all" is contradicted by execution: in the stage-0 lab box a root shell running ./s.sh, where s.sh is -rw------- (no execute bit), gets "sh: ./s.sh: Permission denied", exit 126. Root is exempt from these bits when reading and writing (root read and appended to a mode-000 file and read a mode-600 file owned by uid 1000), not when executing. The rest of the sentence — root would read the file even if someone else owned it — is verified.
issues.quote: the operating system does not apply these permissions to `root` at all — it would read the file even if someone else owned it
issues.fix: Bound the exemption to what the lesson shows: "the operating system does not apply these permissions to `root` when it reads or writes a file — it would read this file even if someone else owned it."

issues.text: The causal chain holds only when the line contains a single word. The stray byte joins the LAST word of the line, which is the command name only in the one-word case. Lab box: `pwd\r` gives "$'pwd\r': command not found"; `ls /tmp/probe/f.txt\r` finds `ls` and fails on the argument — "ls: cannot access '/tmp/probe/f.txt'$'\r': No such file or directory". As written the sentence promises the wrong symptom for any line with arguments. "Reads it one line at a time" also oversimplifies (a shell parses commands, which may span lines) and has no citable source in versions.yaml.
issues.quote: reads it one line at a time and looks up the first word of a line as the name of the thing to run, so a byte another system leaves at the end of that line stays glued to the last word, and the name looked up is not the name you can see
issues.fix: Rewrite as: "A program that runs a script takes the first word of each command line as the name of the thing to run, so a byte another system leaves at the end of a line stays glued to the last word on it — the command name itself when the line holds only one word, and then the name looked up is not the name you can see."

issues.text: Unlisted claim: "this builds and runs the console project in that folder". The `--` half of this sentence is claim 21 and the resolution result is claim 10, but nothing in the ledger records that `dotnet run` builds before it runs. It is true for the pinned version — dotnet-run.md: "The command depends on the dotnet build command to build the code" — so this is a bookkeeping gap, not a wrong statement.
issues.quote: this builds and runs the console project in that folder
issues.fix: Extend claim 21 (or add a claim) with: "In .NET 10, `dotnet run` builds the project before running it (it depends on `dotnet build`), unless `--no-build` is given." source_hint: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/core/tools/dotnet-run, Description.

beyond_scope: Windows rooted-but-relative paths ("one that starts with a bare separator on Windows") in section 4 — the outline says only that a path is absolute or relative to the working directory; this Windows-only sub-case is detail an L1 reader cannot use, and it is stated incorrectly (see the major issue).

issues.text: `root` arrives as a plain fact and then carries a rule I cannot check. First it is a name printed by `whoami`, then it is the one user permissions do not apply to. I have never met the word, so I have to accept on faith both that some users are special and that this one is. It is also the reason the read after `chmod 600` succeeds, which is the surprising part of the whole output block.
issues.fix: Add half a sentence at the first use of the word: `root` is the one user on a Linux machine that the operating system does not check against a file's permissions.
issues.quote: This run still reads the file afterwards because `whoami` says the process runs as `root`, and the operating system does not apply these permissions to `root` at all

issues.text: I cannot read `-rw-r--r--` or `-rw-------`. Core concepts told me a file records "for each kind of user, which of reading, writing and executing is allowed", but nothing says those ten characters are that record, or how they are grouped. So I cannot check the claim that the second one "leaves no access at all for any other ordinary user" — I am told the conclusion and shown a string I cannot connect to it. Quiz q4 option a asks me to notice exactly this string.
issues.fix: Add one sentence before "On this machine…": after the first character, the letters come in groups — the owner's three first, other users' after — and each group shows reading, writing and executing, with a dash where it is not allowed.
issues.quote: `chmod 600` narrows that line to `-rw-------`, which leaves no access at all for any other ordinary user

issues.text: "The small Linux machine that `scripts/up.sh` starts" assumes I know that a script can start a machine, what kind of machine it is, and how to get onto it. The lesson kindly says I need not run it, but quiz q4 opens with "You run `scripts/computer/permissions.sh` on the small Linux machine `scripts/up.sh` starts", so the quiz puts me somewhere the lesson never took me.
issues.fix: Add one clause at that first mention saying what the machine is in the reader's terms (a Linux machine the example repository starts for you with one command), or move this lesson after the lesson that introduces `scripts/up.sh`.
issues.quote: It runs on the small Linux machine that `scripts/up.sh` starts, and you do not have to run it yourself

issues.text: This paragraph jumps from A to C twice. It never says the file came from another system, so "a byte another system leaves" appears out of nowhere — which system, which byte, and why is there a byte at the end of a line at all? And it assumes I know that a script's lines are read as names of things to run, which is a whole model I have never seen. I only learn in Beginners often think that a Windows tool writes one byte more per line, which is the missing middle step.
issues.fix: Add one sentence before it: a tool on one system can end each line of a text file with a different number of bytes than a tool on another, and copying the file carries those bytes across unchanged. Then keep the existing sentence.
issues.quote: so a byte another system leaves at the end of that line stays glued to the last word, and the name looked up is not the name you can see

issues.text: The number 600 is never connected to the string it produces. I can see in the output that after `chmod 600` the line reads `-rw-------`, but I could not predict that, nor pick a number to ask for anything else, so the step feels like a magic word.

issues.text: The prose says `stat` "reports what the file system records about it", but `-c '%A %U:%G %n'` is left as is, so I cannot tell which piece of `-rw-r--r-- root:root app.conf` came from which letter, or whether I could ask for something else.
